A customer's monthly statement says the balance is 750.00, but the lines printed under it add up to 1,250.00. The export reads the total and then the lines inside one transaction, so its author assumed both queries saw the same data. In a test on SQL Server 2022 with two sessions, session A began a transaction at the default level and read the total: 750.00. Session B then inserted a 500.00 payment and committed. Session A read the lines: 4 of them, summing to 1,250.00. Turning on
The belief: inside a transaction, every query sees the same frozen snapshot of the database, from start to finish.

It sounds like what the I in ACID should mean, and the word "transaction" suggests one indivisible moment. Local testing reinforces it: with one user and no concurrent writes, nothing changes between two queries. Even the vocabulary helps: SQL Server's default can run on row versions and has "snapshot" in its option name, and some levels really do work this way. The default just isn't one of them.
The default gives each statement its own view
Microsoft's reference says it directly: at
, data can be changed by other transactions between individual statements within the current transaction, resulting in nonrepeatable reads or phantom data, and this is the SQL Server default. With
on, each statement gets a consistent snapshot as of the start of that statement, not of the transaction. PostgreSQL, whose default is also Read Committed, warns that two successive
commands can see different data even within a single transaction. The statement in the hook hit a

items.text: Dirty read: you read another transaction's uncommitted change, which may still be rolled back.
Nonrepeatable read: you read a row twice and get different values, because someone committed in between.
Phantom: you run the same query twice and get a different set of rows.
: two transactions read the same data, each changes a different row based on what it read, and together they break a rule neither broke alone.

content.text: PostgreSQL implements three distinct levels: its Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed, and its Repeatable Read is snapshot-based and doesn't allow phantoms either. That's from PostgreSQL's docs; the tests in this article ran on SQL Server only.

: Microsoft's docs say so, and in the test a transaction that hadn't read anything yet saw a payment committed after it began. But a frozen view isn't the same as running one at a time. Berenson and colleagues' 1995 critique of the ANSI isolation levels puts it precisely: "Snapshot Isolation is non-serializable because a transaction's Reads come at one instant and the Writes at another." content.text: Snapshot fixes reads that must agree with each other. It doesn't fix decisions. In this test, a hospital rule says at least one doctor stays on call, and two sessions ran the same check at the same time:

blocks.code:
-- Session A (Hany, DoctorId 1) and session B (Laila, DoctorId 2) each ran:
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.OnCall WHERE IsOnCall = 1; -- A saw 2, then B saw 2
UPDATE dbo.OnCall SET IsOnCall = 0 WHERE DoctorId = 1; -- B used DoctorId 2
COMMIT; -- both committed: 0 doctors on call
-- Under SERIALIZABLE: A's UPDATE waited, B's UPDATE made A the
-- deadlock victim (Msg 1205), and Hany stayed on call

, SQL Server's range locks turned the race into a deadlock and rolled one session back; deadlocks get their own article later in this path. PostgreSQL's Serializable is built differently, as Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which adds checks for serialization anomalies on top of snapshots, and its docs say the losing transaction fails with a serialization failure. Both docs say the same thing in different words: be ready to retry.

, the database keeps the result correct by failing one of two conflicting transactions. Code that doesn't catch the error and rerun the whole transaction, reads included, turns a correctness guarantee into a failed request.
Leave the default for ordinary requests. Use
for reports and exports whose queries must agree, and
only around decisions that depend on rows other transactions might change, with a retry around it. Lost updates in read-modify-write code are a separate problem with their own article.
How to apply it in your project
Look for code that reads, then reads again or reads and then decides: statements, exports, balance checks, capacity checks. Those are the places a moving database shows.
